title: Lucas Rodrigues praises win and highlights Brazil's control v Denmark - Yahoo Sports
content: Lucas Rodrigues scored his first goal for the Under-20 National TeamCredits: Nelson Terme /CBF Lucas Rodrigues, of Goiás, had plenty of reasons to celebrate after the Brazil Under-20 National Team's opening match in the series of friendlies in Spain. The midfielder, who scored Brazil's second goal in the 4-1 win over Denmark on Monday (28) at Pinatar Arena, spoke about the joy of finding the net. "I'm very happy about the goal and the win as well. It's an indescribable feeling to represent our country, especially being able to contribute. So I'm very happy. I can only thank God and the coach for the opportunity," he said. Lucas scored in the 35th minute of the first half, when Brazil regained the lead after conceding the equalizer. The midfielder received the ball in the middle third and hit a powerful shot, giving the Danish goalkeeper no chance. For Lucas, the team's strong start was important in helping Brazil build confidence and maintain control of the game. "We started the game really well and managed to score our first goal. We were able to control the game almost the entire time, so that gave the team some confidence," he assessed. The win was the first of three matches for the Under-20 National Team during this FIFA window. After Denmark, Brazil will face the United States and Mexico in matches that Lucas considers important for continuing the team's work. "And we keep improving, keep evolving, because this win is very important. Now we'll keep working, adjust what the coach needs to adjust, and continue this progress," he concluded. The Brazil Under-20 National Team's next match will be against the United States on Thursday (October 1), at 6 p.m. local time and 1 p.m. Brasília time, once again at Pinatar Arena in San Pedro del Pinatar, Spain. The match will be the second of the three friendlies scheduled for this FIFA window. The last one will be against Mexico on October 5, at 11 a.m. local time and 6 a.m. Brasília time, at the same venue. This article was translated into English by Artificial Intelligence. title: Is Czech Republic v England on TV? Channel, kick-off time and how to watch Nations League clash - Yahoo Sports
content: England will look to bounce back from the disappointment of defeat to Spain over the weekend as they continue their Nations League campaign by heading to Prague to take on Czech Republic. There was plenty of good from the Three Lions in a rollercoaster clash with the world champions at a sold-out Wembley on Saturday evening but the defending was borderline negligent at points as they fell to a 3-2 loss. In his pre-match press conference ahead of the clash at the Fortuna Arena, Thomas Tuchel was adamant that "it's a bit early for a 'must win'" game but another loss will not only put a huge dent in England's Nations League hopes but raise further questions over the direction of the team under Tuchel himself. The frustration of the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina, and the bad taste created by Tuchel's substitutions in that loss, still loom large, so a palate-cleansing victory over a side led by new coach Santi Denia would be most welcome for fans. Here's everything you need to know about the clash: Czech Republic v England is due to kick off at 7.45pm BST on Tuesday 29 September at the Fortuna Arena in Prague. Viewers in the United Kingdom can watch the match live on ITV1, with coverage from 7pm BST. A live stream will be available via ITVX. Man City star Nico O'Reilly, who was guilty of a lax pass for Spain's second goal at the weekend, and fellow defender Ezri Konsa are both doubts for the fixture after missing training on the eve of the fixture. "They need to be assessed and take a decision Tuesday morning," said Tuchel of the duo's availability. "Ideally I would love to put the same team out there. I need to speak with the doctors, physios and the players themselves, see what is responsible and what's not, then let's see." Nico O'Reilly is a doubt for the game against the Czech Republic (Getty) The remaining 22 members of the squad were in group training as normal on Monday after Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento all withdrew from the squad last month due to a mixture of injury and load management. Tuchel's comments potentially suggest minimal changes to the starting XI from the Spain clash, with the boss having confirmed after that game that James Trafford will continue in goal for the Czech Republic encounter, before Jordan Pickford takes the gloves for the remaining two matches in this international window. One decision could come at right-back as the German mulls whether to continue with Jarell Quansah or whether this is the right time to reintegrate Real Madrid's Trent Alexander-Arnold into the side. At left-back, Lewis Hall will likely come in if O'Reilly is unable to play, while Jarrad Branthwaite is an option instead of Konsa if required. Potential England XI: Trafford; Quansah, Guehi, Konsa, Hall; Anderson, Lewis-Skelly; Saka, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane

Practical insights from and foracademics and university staff Everything you need for each stepof your study abroad journey Australian university chancellors are set to come under the auspices of the representative body for university executives, as the sector strives to satisfy “heightened expectations” around its governance, accountability and performance. The University Chancellors Council (UCC), which represents the heads of the governing bodies of 39 institutions, is to disband at the end of October. Its duties will be absorbed by Universities Australia (UA), which says the “expanded mandate” will strengthen its role in lifting governance capability. UA chair Carolyn Evans said that as publicly funded institutions, universities had a responsibility to maintain high standards. “This change reflects our shared commitment to ensuring they are well governed, well represented and well placed to meet the expectations of the communities we serve,” she said. “Bringing chancellors and vice-chancellors together gives us a stronger platform for collaboration and a more unified national voice.” Under a new constitution, the UA Board will continue to be chaired by a vice-chancellor. The board will also comprise the CEO and 10 other directors, including seven vice-chancellors and three chancellors. The board’s new University Governance Committee will be chaired by one of the three chancellor directors. These three roles will be filled in an interim capacity by John Hood, Sandra McPhee and Diane Smith-Gander – respectively the chancellors of Flinders, Western Australia and Southern Cross universities – pending ratification of a board election early next year. UCC convenor John Pollaers said the two bodies had worked closely together to shape the new arrangements. “Bringing chancellors and vice-chancellors together strengthens our collective leadership of the sector,” he said. “It carries forward the work of the UCC while building our capacity to strengthen governance, anticipate emerging issues and maintain public confidence in Australian universities.” While Pollaers has courted criticism of his personal style, he has been a staunch internal advocate for governance reform. He supported proposals from the academic union and postgraduate students’ representative body to increase the number of elected positions on Victorian universities’ councils. Pollaers has counselled chancellors to engage more with their critics and to deal more proactively with “systemic” issues – such as wage underpayment – that fuel acute resentment. He has also pressed governing bodies to assert their role more assiduously by demanding accountability from management without crossing the line into “doing management’s job”. Governance expert Hilary Winchester said a merger of the representative arrangements for chancellors and vice-chancellors had been “discussed for a while”, although vice-chancellors had resisted it. “The executive and the governance are pretty different,” said Winchester, a higher education quality consultant who has held senior posts at five universities. “They have shared concerns about finance and buildings and risk and so on, but they do such different things.” She said functioning as a common representative body could present difficulties if UA found itself required to advocate on issues over which chancellors and vice-chancellors were at loggerheads. But this was not so much a conflict as an added complexity for UA, which already represents disparate interest groups. “It’s really hard to speak with one voice, and now you’ve got another potential axis of division,” she said. The body’s CEO, Luke Sheehy, said the new arrangements would strengthen its ability to support universities. “UA’s job is to help universities deliver for Australia," he said. “This change broadens the expertise and capability we can bring to that task.” State government would have firmer hand on universities’ operations under recommendations from latest inquiry into sector ‘crisis’ Intellectual disagreements, broader societal problems and ‘governance 101’ are being misconstrued as blunders, Carolyn Evans claims Representative body for country’s eight institutions loses staff and has functions scaled back with policy work being taken on by in-house teams Sham and shortcut consultations frowned on, as Canberra mulls more governance reforms Scandals about franchised provision have undermined the sector, and universities need to ensure failings are not repeated, vice-chancellors say Vice-chancellor turned PhD student says university executives can feel ‘isolated’ and are seen as having gone to the ‘dark side’ State government would have firmer hand on universities’ operations under recommendations from latest inquiry into sector ‘crisis’ No amount of executive coaching can compensate for a role whose incumbents are accountable for what they can’t fully control, says Vicki L. title: Efinix Announces New Sapphire RV64 SoC, Bringing 64-Bit RISC-V Performance to Embedded FPGA Designs - embeddedcomputing.com
content: Cupertino, Calif., September 28, 2026 – Efinix Inc. announced the Sapphire RV64 SoC, a 64-bit RISC-V processor core expanding the company's Sapphire SoC suite for high-performance, configurable processing and low-power footprint. Built on the RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), Sapphire RV64 is designed for customers whose applications have outgrown the performance, memory, cache, and I/O limits of 32-bit embedded cores but still need the flexibility and low-power capabilities of an FPGA. Sapphire RV64 extends the architecture of Efinix's existing 32-bit Sapphire RV32 SoC: The Sapphire RV64 SoC joins Efinix's existing lineup of 32-bit Sapphire cores, giving designers a full range of options from sub-4K-LE microcontroller sizes up to 64-bit, multi-gigabyte-memory footprint, and high-performance compute capabilities. Common to the existing RV32 architecture, the custom instruction capability delivers FPGA acceleration for edge AI. Sapphire RV64 is available for all Titanium FPGAs, all Topaz FPGAs, and all Trion devices (T20 and above). All Sapphire SoC cores, 32-bit and 64-bit alike, are configured through the Efinity IP Manager and supported by the Efinity Integrated Development Environment, delivering a complete RTL-to-bitstream design flow, along with the Eclipse-based Efinity RISC-V Embedded Software IDE for software development, debugging, and BSP integration. title: The Pentagon Says Every V-22 Osprey Gets A New Gearbox By 2027, But The Math Says Otherwise - Simple Flying
content:
Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso. His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy.

He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture. This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems.

Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future. The Pentagon wants every Bell/Boeing V-22 Osprey to receive a new gearbox by 2027; however, at a production rate of 12 units per month, the math quietly raises questions about whether that goal is achievable. The issue is significant because the Osprey has transformed     military aviation by combining the vertical takeoff and landing capabilities of a helicopter with the speed and range of a conventional turboprop aircraft. At the heart of this capability is its highly complex drive system and massive proprotor gearbox. Weighing around 2,600 pounds, the gearbox transfers power from the engines to the Osprey's proprotors while reducing rotational speed and increasing torque. However, years of failures have made it one of the aircraft's most significant reliability concerns. The V-22, which reached initial operating capability in 2007, is an aircraft with the unique ability to take off, land, and fly vertically like a helicopter or fly like a conventional prop-driven airplane. This ability to transition seamlessly between these two modes of flight comes from its highly complex transmission. Each Osprey's entire drive system weighs about 3,780 pounds (1,715 kg), and the gearbox is central to the aircraft's ability to transition between vertical and conventional flight, according to The Air Current. Of the nearly 4,000 pounds mentioned earlier, the gearbox weighs 2,600 pounds, or 70% of the total weight, plus tilt-axis and mid-wing gearboxes. This system also includes tilt-axis and mid-wing gearboxes and an interconnecting shafting system. This complex design is necessary in order to transfer power from the engine to its massive proprotors. The proprotor gearboxes transfer power from the     Rolls-Royce AE 1107C engines while reducing the engines' high rotational speed and increasing torque to a level suitable for driving the proprotors. This process relies on multiple gear assemblies, including high- and low-speed planetary assemblies containing numerous pinion gears. The system's complexity is particularly relevant given the V-22's gearbox reliability issues. The high-speed planetary assembly contains five pinion gears, while the low-speed assembly contains six, providing some redundancy. Testing and previous inflight failures show the gearbox can continue operating with a cracked pinion, provided the damage does not cause additional failures. According to The Stratos Brief the US military has approximately 403–420 V-22s in service across the services, with 323 MV-22Bs flying with the Marines, 29-41 CMV-22Bs with the Navy, and 51-56 CV-22s deployed with the Air Force's Special Operations Command. While the aircraft has made its way across the US military in just four short years, 20 service members have lost their lives, and four aircraft have been destroyed in 12 V-22 Class A mishaps, according to The Aviationist. The latter represents the most severe class of mishap and includes incidents resulting in a fatality, permanent disability, property damage exceeding $2.5 million, or the complete destruction of an aircraft. The most serious incident occurred on November 29, 2023, near Yakushima Island,     Japan, which resulted in the loss of eight Airmen after the Osprey plunged into the water. The tragic crash led to a three-month safety stand-down of about 400 V-22s, according to The Aviationist. The subsequent Aircraft Accident Investigation Board determined that the proprotor gearbox suffered a catastrophic failure. Investigators speculated that the failure may have resulted from an inclusion—a foreign substance within the steel components that creates a weak point. Regarding gearbox-specific issues, a Navy review identified two primary problems, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine.The first is hard clutch engagements, which occur when the clutch slips and reengages and cause immense torque swings that can make the aircraft difficult to control. The second, and a persistent issue, is the X-53 steel alloy used in most gearbox gears, which make up a significant portion of the aircraft's weight. More than 6,200 shaft horsepower per engine (More than 4,623 kW per engine) Maximum gross 60,500 pounds (27,442 kg) (self-deployment); 57,000 pounds (25,855 kg) (STOL); 52,600 pounds (23,859 kg) (VTOL) Combat radius of 500 nautical miles (926 km) with one internal auxiliary fuel tank 24 personnel (seated), 32 personnel (floor loaded) or 10,000 (4,536 kg) pounds of cargo The alloy contains material impurities or inclusions that lead to part failures; the Navy review found that since 2006, there have been 22 instances of gear failures due to cracking caused by inclusions. In most cases studied in the review, investigators noted that failed gears made from X-53 alloy produced metal chips that caused further operational issues. Regarding the notable mishaps with the Osprey fleet, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that serious accident rates for the Air Force and Marine Corps — the largest operator of the aircraft — increased during fiscal years 2023 and 2024. This was compared to their averages over the preceding eight years; the GAO also found that, depending on the service, the incident rate increased from 36 to 88%. These incidents also affect readiness, since after any malfunction or failure, the associated V-22 must be pulled off the flight line, inspected, repaired, and recertified. Naval Air Systems Command stated that the Osprey had "a low average readiness and availability level in the 2020-2024 timeframe at 50% for the U.S. Navy and AFSOC, and 60%," according to The Aviationist. Marine Corps aviation stands at the forefront of expeditionary air power, check out the top 10 aircraft that the Marines rely on in 2025. The Osprey has become a cornerstone of tactical mobility within the fleet, Marine assault operations, and Air Force special operations. The services need to rely on the aircraft to perform, whether in combat or in any other situation in which it may be called upon. And the 2023 incident near Yakushima Island was surely a tipping point, and fortunately, the gearbox issue is now being remedied. Brigadier General David C. Walsh (USMC) is the Program Executive Officer for Air Anti-Submarine Warfare, Assault & Special Mission Programs. That office is within Naval Air Systems Command and directly manages the V-22 program. According to Defense.Info, General Walsh confirmed that the new gearboxes are currently being manufactured at a rate of 12 per month, and they are being distributed to all three services. Regarding the Navy and Air Force, the retrofit will be complete within the next couple of years, with the latter intending to allocate $213 million (£157.3 million) for the 2027 CV-22 modernization initiatives, and the Marine Corps will follow a similar timeline. This represents a fully funded, systematic upgrade across the entire V-22 fleet. However, at a production rate of 12 new gearboxes per month, the program would produce 144 gearboxes per year. With 469 V-22s currently in service and each aircraft requiring two proprotor gearboxes, replacing both across the fleet would require 938 units. Even allowing for aircraft that have already received the new gearbox and production that began before 2027, the numbers show why reaching the entire fleet on that timeline could conflict with the program's expected goals. The new gearboxes, manufactured from X-53 triple-melt steel, initially began entering repair bays in January 2026. The new steel alloy will provide significantly enhanced resistance to the impurities that have plagued the Osprey's gearboxes, made from double-melt alloy, for the last two decades. "Our analysis shows that going from the double-melt gears to the triple-melt gears will reduce the probability of this happening by an order of magnitude," Admiral John E. Dougherty IV (USN), Commander, Naval Air Systems Command, said, according to Defense.Info. "It will actually take this risk from a serious risk down to a medium risk." Echoing this, Colonel Robert Hurst (USMC), head of the V-22 Joint Program Office, said the new alloy is expected to reduce inclusions in the material by roughly 90%, according to The Aviationist. The C-17 Globemaster III's four-engine design holds the key to its unrivaled capabilities, but was this a choice of power or necessity? The V-22’s gearbox has become a critical focus for the services after years of failures and readiness concerns. The 2023 Yakushima Island crash, which claimed eight Airmen, underscored the consequences of a catastrophic gearbox failure and helped drive efforts to address the problems with the X-53 alloy. According to Air & Space Forces Magazine, a 2024 CV-22 mishap further illustrated the issue, with investigators finding an inclusion measuring just 0.055 inches long by 0.011 inches wide in the failed gear. The new triple-melt steel gearboxes offer a major improvement, with NAVAIR estimating an order-of-magnitude reduction in the probability of inclusion-related failures. However, with production running at 12 gearboxes per month, questions remain about how quickly the fleet can receive the upgraded components. title: Trust Fund Recovery Penalty Willfulness and the Capping Effect of Corporate Offers-in-Compromise: A Technical Analysis of Amodio v. Commissioner - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Amodio v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-96, Docket No. 9959-22L (Sept. 28, 2026) For tax controversy practitioners, Certified Public Accountants, and Enrolled Agents, navigating the personal liability provisions of Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 6672 requires a precise understanding of the statutory standards for “willfulness” and the joint-and-several mechanisms governing the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (TFRP). In Amodio v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-96 (Sept. 28, 2026), Special Trial Judge Carluzzo delivered an instructive opinion examining two pivotal tax controversy issues: (1) whether a corporate officer acts “willfully” under I.R.C. § 6672(a) when, upon discovering pre-existing tax delinquencies, he uses unencumbered corporate funds to pay net wages and union benefits to maintain business operations, and (2) whether an Offer-in-Compromise (OIC) accepted by the IRS to compromise the underlying corporate employment tax debt operates to cap the individual officer’s derivative TFRP liability. This article examines the factual matrix of Amodio, dissects the taxpayer’s statutory arguments, outlines the Tax Court’s legal analysis, and evaluates the judicial synthesis of joint-and-several tax principles against Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) administrative guidelines. The petitioner, Thomas Amodio, resided in New York at the time the petition was filed. Before organizing Creative Solutions, Inc. (Creative) in 2002, Amodio worked as a carpenter. Through Creative, he provided specialized construction services focused on retail display cases and millwork installation. Creative operated as a “union shop,” employing unionized trade laborers in the New York and New Jersey metropolitan areas. Consequently, in addition to union-negotiated wage scales, Creative was contractually mandated to pay various employee union fringe benefits. During 2015 and 2016, Creative encountered severe financial strain stemming from “a slow-paying major client, coupled with union demands.” This cash flow deficit precipitated the nonpayment of federal employment taxes (Form 941 withheld income tax and employee Federal Insurance Contributions Act [FICA] taxes). Significantly, the initial decision to withhold payment of federal employment taxes to alleviate corporate liquidity pressures was made by Creative’s office manager and a third-party payroll processing firm, without Amodio’s knowledge or direct authorization. As noted by the Tax Court, “Petitioner became aware of the failure after the fact.” Upon discovering the outstanding trust fund delinquencies, Amodio directed available corporate revenues toward paying employee net wages, union benefit contributions, and key suppliers to keep the business operational. Amodio recognized that failing to satisfy employee wage and union benefit obligations would prompt trade unions to immediately pull their workers from active job sites, terminating ongoing projects and destroying Creative’s commercial viability. On July 28, 2020, Creative successfully entered into an Offer-in-Compromise with the IRS pursuant to I.R.C. § 7122. The corporate OIC resulted in the satisfaction, in whole or in part, of Creative’s employment tax obligations for multiple tax periods, including the calendar quarters ended December 31, 2015, and December 31, 2016. Following the corporate tax defaults, the IRS assessed individual TFRPs against Amodio pursuant to I.R.C. § 6672 for the tax quarters ended December 31, 2015, June 30, 2016, September 30, 2016, and December 31, 2016. Amodio subsequently paid off the assessed liabilities for certain intermediate quarters, leaving the periods ended December 31, 2015, and December 31, 2016, in dispute. On April 4, 2022, the IRS Office of Appeals issued a Notice of Determination Concerning Collection Action(s) Under Section 6320 and/or 6330 (Notice), sustaining a proposed levy action to collect Amodio’s outstanding individual TFRP liabilities for the remaining two quarters. Amodio timely filed a petition with the United States Tax Court under I.R.C. § 6330(d). In his Tax Court petition and trial presentation, Amodio requested relief from the proposed collection action on two primary legal grounds: In a Collection Due Process (CDP) proceeding governed by I.R.C. § 6330(d), where the validity or amount of the underlying tax liability is properly at issue, the Tax Court reviews the Commissioner’s determination under a de novo standard (Sego v. Commissioner, 114 T.C. 604, 610 (2000); Goza v. Commissioner, 114 T.C. 176, 181–82 (2000)). The Court confirmed that the IRS complied with procedural statutory mandates, including obtaining timely managerial supervisory approval for penalty assessment pursuant to I.R.C. § 6751(b). In challenging the existence or amount of an underlying TFRP liability, the taxpayer bears the legal burden of proof under Tax Court Rule 142(a) (Thompson v. Commissioner, 140 T.C. 173, 178 (2013); Malloy v. United States, 17 F.3d 329, 331 (11th Cir. 1994); Hochstein v. United States, 900 F.2d 543, 548 (2d Cir. 1990)). Under I.R.C. § 6672(a), “[a]ny person required to collect, truthfully account for, and pay over” any federal tax who “willfully fails” to do so is liable for a penalty equal to the total amount of the tax evaded, not collected, or not accounted for and paid over (Kalb v. United States, 505 F.2d 506, 510–11 (2d Cir. 1974); Mason v. Commissioner, 132 T.C. 301, 321 (2009)). Amodio conceded that he was a “person” within the statutory definition of I.R.C. § 6671(b). Addressing the statutory requirement of “willfulness,” the Tax Court reaffirmed established jurisprudence holding that a willful failure constitutes “a voluntary, conscious and intentional failure to collect, truthfully account for, and pay” employment taxes (Newsome v. United States, 431 F.2d 742, 745 (5th Cir. 1970); Mason, 132 T.C. at 324–25; Winter v. United States, 196 F.3d 339, 345 (2d Cir. 1999)). Bad motive, evil intent, or intent to defraud the government is not required. Special Trial Judge Carluzzo articulated the established rule governing post-discovery conduct: “Quite simply for purposes of section 6672, willfulness is demonstrated if a ‘person,’ after becoming aware of a corporation’s outstanding employment taxes, uses unencumbered corporate funds for purposes other than paying the corporation’s outstanding employment taxes.” (United States v. Rem, 38 F.3d 634, 643 (2d Cir. 1994); Mason, 132 T.C. at 325; Gustin v. United States, 876 F.2d 485, 492 (5th Cir. 1989)). Applying this standard, the Court acknowledged the real-world economic pressures faced by business owners attempting to satisfy employee wages and union mandates during cash flow bottlenecks. However, the Court rejected Amodio’s defense that commercial necessity or union pressure negates willfulness under tax law: “Using withheld employment taxes to ease cashflow problems has consequences, which is one reason this Opinion is being written.” The Court relied directly on Second Circuit precedent establishing that employees and trade unions holding wage claims enjoy no statutory priority over federal trust fund obligations: “While working around cashflow disruptions to ensure timely payment to employees is understandable, for purposes of determining willfulness, ‘an employee to whom the corporate employer owes wages is simply another creditor.’” (Hochstein v. United States, 900 F.2d 543, 548 (2d Cir. 1990)). Because Amodio learned of the trust fund deficiencies shortly after assessment and subsequently chose to disburse corporate funds to pay net wages, union benefits, and operational expenses rather than satisfying the delinquent employment taxes, the Tax Court concluded that his failure to pay was willful under I.R.C. § 6672(a). Having established Amodio’s liability under I.R.C. § 6672(a), the Court turned to the central legal controversy: whether Creative’s corporate Offer-in-Compromise restricts the amount the IRS can collect from Amodio individually. The Court began its analysis by reiterating the foundational nature of Section 6672 penalties as derivative and joint-and-several obligations: “Penalties contemplated by section 6672(a) are, by nature, derivative of a different taxpayer’s failure to satisfy its employment tax obligations. The employment tax liability of the other taxpayer and the person described in section 6671 is joint and several, like the income tax liability that results from the election to file a joint federal income tax return by married individuals.” From this premise, Special Trial Judge Carluzzo underscored the bedrock doctrine prohibiting double tax collection: “It almost goes without saying that the Commissioner can collect a joint and several tax liability only once, a point so fundamental it is not even discussed in the brief of either party.” (Brown v. United States, 591 F.2d 1136, 1142 (5th Cir. 1979)). The Commissioner argued that under Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) provisions—specifically IRM 5.8.4.22.1(2) (May 10, 2013) (currently IRM 5.8.4.21.1(2) [Apr. 25, 2025])—the settlement of a corporate tax liability through an OIC does not extinguish the individual responsible person’s TFRP, enabling the IRS to levy against the responsible officer for the full uncompromised balance. Respondent further asserted that the Tax Court had “favorably” commented on this IRM provision in Mason v. Commissioner. Special Trial Judge Carluzzo firmly rejected the Commissioner’s position and clarified the misinterpretation of Mason: “Not so fast, according to respondent. As respondent views the matter, the excess of petitioner’s TFRP for each of those periods over Creative’s offer-in-compromise-reduced employment tax liability remains due and collectable by levy. Yet another reason this Opinion is being written.” The Court highlighted that footnote 19 in Mason referenced the IRM merely as an expression of internal administrative policy, explicitly noting that the handling of the corporate OIC had “no direct bearing” on that taxpayer’s case (Mason, 132 T.C. at 329 & n.19). The IRM does not carry the force of law and cannot override general legal principles governing joint-and-several debt satisfaction. Rejecting respondent’s administrative argument, Special Trial Judge Carluzzo held: “There might be circumstances that ‘may’ support respondent’s decision to collect from a responsible person a TFRP liability that exceeds a corporation’s related employment tax liability that has been adjusted by an offer-in-compromise, but in the absence of a specific reason for doing so in this case we are more persuaded to proceed by applying common sense and the general principles that govern joint and several federal tax liabilities.” Synthesizing the statutory framework and common-law principles of joint-and-several liability, the Tax Court arrived at two core findings: Willfulness Established: Amodio’s deliberate choice to pay employee wages and union benefits after gaining knowledge of Creative’s trust fund tax defaults met the statutory standard for willfulness under I.R.C. § 6672(a). Collection Amount Capped by Corporate OIC: Respondent’s collection authority under the Notice of Determination must be legally capped at the compromised corporate balance: “In so doing, it follows and we hold that respondent may proceed with collection as determined in the Notice but only in amounts that do not exceed the amount of Creative’s employment tax liability for each period in dispute, as adjusted by the offer-in-compromise.” Because the precise remaining balance of Creative’s compromised tax liability could not be fully established from the trial record, the Tax Court ordered that decision be entered under Tax Court Rule 155 to allow the parties to compute the exact capped collection amounts. title: Hilton coach tied Section V's all-time wins record and can break it Friday - Democrat and Chronicle
content: Rich Lipani arrived at the top of the Section V football all-time coaching wins list with a pile of points. Lipani, in his 38th season as Hilton's coach, and 41st overall, picked up his 230th varsity win Sept. 25, when the Cadets rolled to a 54-8 victory over Irondequoit. Dave Whitcomb, the only coach in Section V Football history to win Section V championships with three different teams, also has 230 wins in retirement. "He actually hired me for my first job, the JV coach at Aquinas in 1985," Lipani said. "He was the head coach at Aquinas that year, and I knew him from when I was in high school, he was running a bunch of football camps." Hilton remains undefeated after its fourth victory, perhaps the team's most dominant win this fall. The Cadets rolled to 489 yards of total offense and intercepted three Irondequoit passes. "Maybe one time since last November," Hilton senior offensive lineman Zachary DeMarte said about the number of times Lipani talked about his place in Section V Football history. The next chance for the Cadets to give Lipani sole possession of the record is Oct. 2, when they play at Webster Schroeder. The Monroe County Division I matchup between teams in Class A1 kicks off at 7 p.m. "I've been doing it a long time," Lipani said. "So, if we didn't have a lot of wins, I'd be doing a crappy job. "It just means that we're 4-0. We're happy to be 4-0, we gotta keep rolling here." title: This GTA V mod lets you destroy Flock cameras. Its creator explains why. - Mashable
content: Los Santos has a new way to get you in trouble, and you don’t even have to commit a crime. A new Grand Theft Auto V mod from artist Morry Kolman, who goes by WTTDOTM online, installs 235 virtual Flock license plate reader cameras around the game’s fictional city. Called Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, or GTALPR, it brings an extra layer of surveillance to your next drive. And because this is GTA, you can destroy the cameras and collect in-game cash from their wreckage. But the opportunity to blow them up is only part of the point. Kolman wants players to feel what happens when a familiar environment becomes a place where they’re constantly being watched. "I’m an artist, and much of my practice is based around giving people interesting and engaging ways to learn about the technological and political world around them," Kolman told Mashable. "GTALPR is very much in that vein." For Kolman, a game modeled on an American city, and familiar to millions of players, offered a way to make surveillance tangible. "Suddenly, you're always watched," he added. "With the simple addition of some cameras, the entire environment gains a new passive layer of hostility." In the real world, Flock’s automated license plate readers capture vehicle images and enable police to search for vehicles and receive alerts about those on watchlists. Flock pitches the technology as a way to help law enforcement locate wanted vehicles. Civil liberties groups, including the ACLU, argue that these networks enable mass surveillance of people going about their everyday lives. Kolman’s virtual version draws directly from the geography of the real network. "I chose 235 for the number of cameras to use in GTALPR because it is 1/10th the amount of Flock cameras currently in LA County, and Los Santos is about 1/10th its real counterparts size," he told Mashable. His project page identifies the community mapping project DeFlock as the source for the camera count. The placements aren’t random, either. Kolman built himself a tool to compare the real and fictional maps, then used it to place cameras in corresponding locations. "The closest comparison is probably the area around Santa Monica Pier vs. Del Perro Pier," he said. The result brings a real-world surveillance footprint into a place players may already know street by street. One of the mod’s most pointed feature kicks in when players haven’t committed a crime. Each time a player passes through a camera’s field of view, there’s a 1-in-20 chance it will trigger an unprovoked police chase to "represent this pattern of false reports, and show that living with this surveillance is not a matter of 'having nothing to hide'... it is simply a matter of 'when will it happen to you,'" Kolman described. His broader argument is that avoiding wrongdoing doesn’t eliminate the risks of being surveilled. He described the mechanic as a challenge to the familiar reassurance that people with "nothing to hide" have nothing to worry about. Players can also dismantle the virtual network. Destroy a camera and collect its remains, and the mod awards $600 in game currency. The reward price is based on the estimated value of the parts inside a real Flock camera, after the group Eyes Off Cedar Rapids took one apart to examine its hardware. There’s also built-in speedrun tracking for destroying the cameras, plus an option to render and save the images they capture — including pictures of players destroying them. It’s an absurd addition to a game already full of opportunities for mayhem, but a fitting one in a country where Flock cameras have made everyday drives part of a searchable surveillance network. As Kolman puts it, "I put Flock cameras in GTA V as a way to highlight and make tangible the pervasive intrusion of Flock and other ALPR cameras into daily American life via a game that is based on an American city and that millions of my fellow citizens are intimately familiar with." The mod and its installation instructions are available through Kolman’s website. Olivia Tauber is the deputy editor of digital culture, covering creators, media, movies, beauty, and more. title: How 2 Ford engineers put a V-10 and a stick shift into a Lincoln - Detroit Free Press
content: If you buy a car, you can do whatever modifications your heart desires if you have the right shop you can trust, or you can build it yourself. Diego Ugaz and Jack Parnoutsoukian, both of Lincoln Park, are two Ford engineers who also are YouTubers on the side who build project cars in their own home garages. Their most exciting build is their Lincoln Continental that features a V-10 engine, manual transmission and rear-wheel drive. Parnoutsoukian and Ugaz met in college at University of California at Davis where they both majored in mechanical engineering. They also worked together on the university's Formula SAE team where UC Davis students along with students around the country built small racecars resembling Formula 1 vehicles. After graduating, they both came to the Motor CIty to work for Ford and have been in Michigan ever since. "We are both from California and graduated from UC Davis and came to Michigan to work for Ford. I work with battery systems and Diego works with brake systems," said Parnoutsoukian. Outside of work, they modified their own cars and other project vehicles they purchased. Then they decided to create a YouTube channel in 2022 called "Build It Yourself," which currently has over 100,000 subscribers. They've done other builds, such as putting a V-8 into a Honda SX200 or K-swapped a Mustang where the Ford got the Honda engine. But beyond grabbing the manual transmission from a Mustang, fitting a Triton V-10 that was originally made for a Ford F-350 into a Lincoln Continental was their toughest challenge yet. Lincoln is well known for being one of the most luxurious American automakers. If you happen to see one of their modern cars or classic vehicles on the road, they aren’t overly flashy and have an elegant look to them. Parnoutsoukian said, "We weren't always Lincoln fans but we always liked how the Continental looked. We thought it didn't get the love it deserved so we decided to make it into something more unique." This led to them coming to the crazy conclusion that the car needed a V-10 engine swap along with a rear-wheel drivetrain and a manual transmission. The car originally came with a V-6 engine, front-wheel drive and a six-speed automatic transmission. A build like this takes a lot of time, effort and money to make changes this drastic. They said it took them a total of 2,000 hours over three years of work. Because the roaring V-10 is the highlight of the car, they had to rebuild the engine three times as it kept breaking down. They said they believe the current setup should last. To put a manual gear shifter into the car to control the new manual instead of automatic transmission, they had to sacrifice their cup holders located in the center stack or under the dashboard as there was nowhere else to put it. They actually had to build some parts for the engine themselves and change the dimensions of the vehicle slightly, in the cabin and under the hood, so everything would fit. "It started with an engine from a F-350, which is a Triton 6.8-liter V-10. All that's left from that is the block and the crank. Everything else we custom-made," said Ugaz. Once the car starts up and the rumbling V-10 gets going, they are reminded by the sound of what they've created. Most Lincolns are calm and quiet and don't make much noise. But Ugaz and Parnoutsoukian's remodel keeps something from the original. Even though the car now has 495 horsepower and shakes while idling, it has an air suspension and still glides on the road in typical Lincoln fashion. When asked how much they would sell it for they said they never even thought about parting ways with it and called it "priceless." They also talked about how the amount of work they put into the car wouldn't be valued as much by a secondhand owner so they would prefer to hold on to this car. Said Ugaz: "Putting a price on it is something we haven't even considered. But the amount of work it took to build this is what makes it special and wouldn't be valued by a secondhand buyer. So we'd rather hold on to it and keep driving it ourselves." Keenan Thompson is a car culture reporter for the Detroit Free Press. Contact Keenan at kthompson@freepress.com. title: Subaru's Forester Costs More To Maintain Than A RAV4 Or CR-V Hybrid, But Beats Both On Reliability - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update Reliability is often the number one concern when buying a family vehicle. Of course, interior space, safety, and amenities matter, too. Nevertheless, raising kids is expensive enough already, and it gets even harder when you spend hundreds of dollars more per year on car maintenance than you would with a different model. The Subaru Forester is one of the safest models you can buy, with the 2026 model earning an IIHS Top Safety Pick+ award. It's roomy, stylish, efficient, and fairly reliable. However, repair data shows it costs more to maintain than its primary competitors, the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V. What about its powertrain creates a paradox: solid reliability that still costs more than its rivals? All specs come directly from the manufacturers. Prices are correct at the time of writing and exclude destination, options, taxes, incentives, and potential dealership fees and markups. Automakers reserve the right to change prices at any time without notice. Although Subaru models are fairly reliable, they tend to cost more to maintain than their Honda and Toyota rivals. The Forester is a prime example. Perhaps this is because its standard symmetrical AWD system requires more frequent maintenance and servicing than rivals' two-wheel-drive systems. Relatively simple tasks for inline-4s, like changing spark plugs, take more time and effort on flat boxer engines because there are two banks of cylinders. That said, the added maintenance difficulty adds up monetarily. According to RepairPal, the Forester costs $632 per year to maintain. The Toyota RAV4 is a couple hundred dollars cheaper per year at $429. The Honda CR-V is the cheapest of these three models at $407 per year. Forester vs RAV4 vs CR-V Maintenance Costs Estimates CarEdge is another reputable source that has a more optimistic outlook. Adding up RepairPal's estimate means buyers would spend roughly $3,160 in five years, but CarEdge says buyers should expect to spend about $2,718 on maintenance and repairs over half a decade. The table above lays out the rest of the data. It may feel backward to say the Forester is more reliable than the other two, even when it costs more to maintain, but the data shows that. Real-world reliability depends heavily on how well you maintain your car. If you don't keep up with regular fluid and filter changes and inspect brake pads, bushings, and other parts, your car might not last as long as rivals, no matter its reputation. That said, the Subaru Forester has data to back up its reliability. JD Power's 2026 Vehicle Dependability Study shows Toyota falling below Subaru and Honda sitting below the industry average. The study counts the number of problems per 100 vehicles (measured as PP100). Subaru earned sixth place overall with 181 PP100, while Toyota earned eighth place with 185 PP100, and Honda fell behind with 211 PP100. JD Power's quality and reliability scores measure only the models' initial quality, so they exclude long-term data. Keep that in mind when you hear that the 2026 Forester was awarded an 81 out of 100. The Toyota RAV4 falls behind with a 77/100, while the Honda CR-V tops both with an 83/100 for the 2026 model year. All three models' current generations are too new (having debuted within the last few years or more recently) to have accrued major reliability data. We can let you know that the 2026 Forester already has three recalls that don't affect reliability. The 2026 CR-V Hybrid and 2026 RAV4 each have one recall, neither of which affects reliability. Now that you know how much you might pay for maintenance over five years of ownership, let's see whether it balances out with each vehicle's initial cost. The Forester is the most affordable of the bunch up front. It's available in ten trims, including gas and hybrid variants, starting with the Base trim at $29,995 and ending with the Touring Hybrid trim at $41,545 before destination and options. Toyota splits its RAV4 into hybrid and plug-in hybrid models. The standard hybrid model is simple, with only six trim levels to choose from. The model starts at $31,900 for the LE trim and ends at $43,300 for the Limited trim before destination. The PHEV starts at $41,500 and ends at $48,500 for the GR Sport. Then there's the Honda CR-V, with seven trims and a mix of gas-only and hybrid variants. The cheapest model is the LX at $30,920, while the most expensive trim is the Sport Touring Hybrid at $42,550. If you're searching for the cheapest hybrid of each model, then the RAV4 wins outright. Subaru comes in second place with its Premium Hybrid trim at $34,730, then Honda sits in last place with the Sport Hybrid at $35,630. Subaru models manage to hold their value better than most brands. In fact, CarEdge data shows the brand has an average resale value after five years on the road of 61.2% of the model's original value. The source places Subaru in second overall, while Toyota earns first place with 64.9% value retention after half a decade, and Honda comes in third place with 60.5% resale value. Individual models rank differently, though. We're not surprised to see the Toyota RAV4, one of the best-selling and most popular vehicles in the country, hold value better than its rivals. According to CarEdge, the RAV4 only loses 28% of its value after five years. By comparison, the CR-V and Forester are slightly worse. Honda's midsize SUV depreciates by 29%, and Subaru's model takes third with 34% depreciation in the same timeframe. Like we mentioned earlier, the Forester is available with both gas-only and hybrid powertrains. The 2.5-liter boxer four-cylinder makes a relatively weak 180 horsepower and 178 lb-ft of torque — our road tester took the 2025 model out for a spin last year and found it adequate for most situations, as long as you're not an aggressive driver. It's a proven unit, but lacks any kind of urgency on the road - it's best not to try and dive into that small traffic gap from a standstill. It's fine for general day-to-day use if you're not a driver who's always hurrying, and the CVT does its job well enough. - Ian Wright, Senior Road Tester, CarBuzz (2025 Subaru Forester First Drive Review) The hybrid option offers a little more pep in its step. It uses the same 2.5-liter boxer engine but adds an electric motor to boost total output to 194 horsepower. The Honda CR-V is also offered with both gas-only and hybrid options; the gas models use a 1.5-liter turbocharged inline-4 that makes 190 hp and 179 lb-ft of torque, while the rest of the trims use a 2.0-liter naturally aspirated inline-4 hybrid system for a total of 204 horsepower. Finally, there's the Toyota RAV4. Buyers can choose either the standard hybrid model, which offers 226 hp in FWD models and 236 hp in AWD models, or the PHEV model, which delivers 320 combined horsepower. Maintenance costs can be daunting for any car owner. Subaru, Toyota, and Honda offer among the most reliable vehicles on the market. Plus, their offerings are generally affordable. Their midsize SUVs: the Forester, RAV4, and CR-V, are some of their most popular models, so there's plenty of data to go around regarding each one's maintenance costs. RepairPal shows the Forester as costing a couple of hundred dollars more per year than its rivals. According to CarEdge, the Forester still costs only a few hundred dollars more to own over five years than the CR-V, while the RAV4 stays under $2,000 for maintenance and repairs. To us, all three are relatively cheap to own. A couple of hundred dollars spread out over twelve months shouldn't affect you much. Robert Vernon Stolting, 96, passed away peacefully on his farm, in West End, on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Robert (Bob) was born in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Dec. 2, 1929, to Jessie Louise Schwerdt and Frederick Carl Stolting. Bob’s formal education culminated at Brooklyn Tech, a prestigious public specialized high school in Brooklyn, N.Y., that focused on science, technology, engineering and mathematics. He started work at Republic Steel, in New York, only to be drafted into the U.S. Army during the Korean War, where he served as supply sergeant in the states. He returned to Republic Steel, later joining Nicholas J. Bouras Inc. at its inception in Summit, N.J., and working there for over 30 years. Bouras Inc. became a prominent steel sales and engineering agent, and Bob enjoyed his role as steel sales engineer for the New York City and Long Island areas, handling products like bar joists and metal decks on commercial buildings. A family man, Bob was predeceased by his parents, Jessie and Frederick Stolting; sister, Muriel Stolting Fleischman; first wife, Evelyn Batch Stolting; and daughter, Kim Stolting Daly. He is survived by his wife, Ruth Pecan Stolting; son, Jeffrey Stolting and wife, Mary; son, Tod Stolting; four grandchildren, Terrence, Matthew, Cassandra (Andie) and Tyler; and great-grandson, Ronin. For over 25 years, he enjoyed his home in Maine where family and friends gathered for sailing, swimming, water skiing, lobster parties and holidays. Bob always loved animals, breeding Dalmatians with his first wife, Evelyn, and raising Vizslas, honeybees and chickens in retirement with his wife Ruth on a tract of land that he named Oldefield Farm. Mentored on the farm by Leonard and Joyce Tufts, descendants of Pinehurst’s founder, Bob learned to appreciate the beauty of the longleaf pine ecosystem in our Sandhills area. The farm was part of the Forest Stewardship Program, and Bob worked the land and became a member of NC Forestry Association, American Forest Foundation, Friends of Plant Conservation, Moore County Beekeepers Association and Livestock Conservancy. An emeritus member of the Master Gardeners of Moore County, Bob gave talks with Ruth on the speakers’ circuit regarding honeybees and the longleaf pine ecosystem, and helped rejuvenate the Moore County Farmers Market, where Oldefield Farm had a space allotted for several years. His passion for the Sandhills induced him to help co- found and serve as vice president for Save Our Sandhills Inc., a nonprofit that was a watchdog for environmental threats, a crusader for the balance of nature, a public educator for our unique ecosystem and a supporter of land use laws. He worked tirelessly to preserve this ecosystem, ultimately adding 60 acres of the family’s farmland to North Carolina’s conservation preserves. A memorial service will be held at 11 a.m., Saturday, Oct. 24, at The Village Chapel in Pinehurst. A live stream will be available at tvcpinehurst.com. In lieu of flowers, remembrances may be made to The Village Chapel or Moore Humane Society. Online condolences may be left at www.bolesfuneralhome.com. title: The Hard Lessons of Springfield - The Bulwark
content: There are plenty of people happy about what is happening to the Haitian community. I’m back from Ohio, where we did a Bulwark LIVE benefit show on Friday night, and I want to talk with you about the experience. Because there were some good lessons and some hard lessons. We’ll start with the good. As of this writing, you guys—the Bulwark community—have raised $351,000 for the Haitian community in Springfield. I am dumbstruck by your generosity. Here’s what that money buys: The Haitian community in Springfield is under siege. People who came to America legally and built productive, beautiful lives now hide in their homes, afraid to go outside because masked, armed agents of the state may abduct them. They cannot go grocery shopping. If they are sick or hurt, they cannot go to the doctor or the hospital. They cannot take their children to school. They need help. And you all stepped up to give it. I am, once again, overwhelmed with gratitude for the goodness in your hearts. Thank you. The singer John Legend sent a message to the show on Friday night and it was powerful. I hope you’ll watch the video because even though it’s six minutes long, it is worth your time. Hello. Years ago, I joined my friend, Skip Gates, on a show called Finding Your Roots, and I learned something about my family that changed the way I think about my home state of Ohio. One of my ancestors, his name was Peyton Polly. He was born into slavery in Kentucky. And when his master passed away, he granted Peyton his freedom in his will. And when Peyton gained that freedom, he brought his family across the Ohio River to build a life in Ohio—a free state. But some people in Peyton’s former master’s family were not happy about this development. And one night in 1850, armed men crossed into Ohio, broke into the Pollys’ home, and kidnapped eight children, carrying them back across the river into slavery. Devastating. But Ohio responded. The governor, the legislature, they took up the cause. They sent investigators and lawyers to fight to bring those children home. Now, I hesitated to tell that story because I don’t want to compare slavery to what’s happening now. It is not the same as the immigration debate we’re having today. But I’ve never forgotten what that family story taught me. One, is that my family has a legacy we can be proud of. But also, that when our neighbors’ freedom, safety, and dignity were in doubt, the state of Ohio stepped up for us. Ohio was a free state, a major part of the Underground Railroad, a place where people sought refuge and freedom. They often found it in Ohio. So in 2026, we have to challenge ourselves. We have to ask the question, what kind of state are we going to be? I want to thank the Bulwark team for making room for this conversation. I want to thank my friend Patrick Gaspard for inviting me to be a part of it. Before I was John Legend, I was a kid growing up in Springfield, Ohio, the son of a factory worker, the son of a seamstress. I learned to sing in the church. I started playing the piano when I was five. Springfield made me. So when I hear Springfield being talked about on national television, I don’t hear a talking point. I don’t see a political football. I see my home! I see my people. Like communities across this country, people in Springfield, they want the basics: good schools, affordable housing, good jobs, health care, safe neighborhoods, a fair shot at building a good life. But when those things feel out of reach, we’re too often told to blame somebody else. That another family has to lose for yours to get ahead. And that opportunity for others is a loss for you. I don’t believe that zero-sum thinking is how we build a stronger Springfield. I don’t believe that’s how we build a stronger America. The Haitian families who came to Springfield, they came looking for safety and a future. Over time, they became classmates, coworkers, business owners, teammates, friends, caregivers, neighbors. Tonight I want to say the name of one of those neighbors, Pierre Damas Bel. Pierre was 20 years old. He came here from Haiti in 2024. He graduated from my high school, Springfield High School, with honors. He played soccer and was active in JROTC. He had just started at Wright State University. He wanted to become a doctor. He should have become a doctor. He should have had so much life ahead of him. Instead, his family is grieving him. To Pierre’s father, his family, his friends, his teammates, his teachers, I send you my love tonight. To every Haitian family in Springfield carrying fear and uncertainty, I send you love. To my hometown, I send you love. And to Ohio, the state that will always be a part of who I am, I send you love. But love has to mean more than what we say. Love has to mean showing up. And everyone here tonight has already done that. Thank you. You are directly supporting the Haitian Support Center and families in Springfield who need help right now. Thank you. And this is about TPS, but it’s also about our entire immigration policy—how we treat people, whether we can hold on to our humanity. We have seen leaders across the aisle in Ohio who do that, and we can too. Tonight we help. In November, we make our voices heard. And always we keep organizing. Keep building coalitions. Keep pushing for a more humane way forward. May Ohio always be the place that it was for my ancestors, a place with a big, beautiful heart. One that welcomes the refugee, extends a helping hand to the stranger, one that fights for freedom and believes in the expansiveness of the American dream. Thank you. This is the way—the only way. We show up for each other. But now, I’m afraid we have to talk about the hard lesson. When we went to Minneapolis last winter we encountered a city and a state united against totalitarianism. Literally every person I met was outraged at what the federal government was doing. Thousands of volunteers organized to help. The governor, the mayor, the local police were all united in trying to protect both citizens and immigrants. I’m sure there were, somewhere in Minnesota, people who celebrated the deaths of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, but they were unwilling to show their faces because they knew, at the instinctual level, that it would make them pariahs in the community. I was only on the ground for a short period of time and it was obvious that there are plenty of people who are happy to see Haitians being criminalized, arrested, and deported. I picked this up from conversations with people who were polite about it, and from remarks made by people who were less polite about it, including people who were unhappy with us doing a show to benefit the Haitian community. And in general, the level of support for the Haitian community has been nothing like the mobilization in Minnesota. There are brave and generous volunteers working to help, but they seem to be the minority. The governor of Ohio has refused to step in—at all—even though his sympathies are obviously with the Haitians. He knows better, but has been cuckolded by his cowardice. On Saturday, the day after our benefit, Nazis marched through Springfield. It was a small group. Maybe a couple dozen black-clad men. But they had two swastika flags and they knew what they were doing. There’s a reason they were marching in Springfield and not Columbus. Also, unlike in Minneapolis, these guys understood that there is a baseline level of support for their position. I wish that Springfield was an uplifting story about the power of community coming together in the face of authoritarianism. But it wasn’t. It’s the story of parts of the community coming together to oppose authoritarianism while other parts stand off to the side either quietly nodding in support of the authoritarians or openly cheering them on. Springfield is a story not about the power of community but about the importance of power. It is not enough to help victims. We also have to organize to fight and win power. And if we get power, we must use it. Without illusions or remorse. Put this on a pillow: If Democrats regain power then every member of the Trump regime should be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law. From Jared Kushner and Corey Lewandowski down to the lowest-level ICE employee. Every business executive who bribed the president, every government employee who got rich, every agent who roughed up an immigrant—they should all live in fear of the law. If there’s evidence that one of these guys jaywalked, or falsified an expense report, or listed a vacation property as a primary residence, they should be facing down a freight train of accountability. No transgression should be too small to sit beneath the notice of the next administration. If we don’t hold these people accountable, then they’ll do it again. I believe this in my bones. If you’re of the same mind, I hope you’ll come ride with us. Because we will never look away from the hard stuff. The first lesson of Springfield is that we can help our neighbors. The second lesson is that this moment is not just the result of a rogue regime operating outside the scope of its mandate. It turns out that many Americans did not know they were fascists—but when the time came, they did indeed find out. I want to be clear about the persecutions of Springfield’s Haitians. These are people who overwhelmingly came here legally. And they have been overwhelmingly law-abiding and productive. The only reason they have not become citizens is because U.S. law did not provide such a pathway. The president and vice president issued blood libels about this community during the 2024 campaign. Subsequently the vice president said, “If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention . . . then that’s what I’m going to do.” The administration then revoked the protected legal status of this community. This is judicially blessed ethnic cleansing motivated by nothing—nothing—other than naked white nationalism. America has a long history of this stuff. John Legend talked about some of it. Free states and slave states; lynchings and kidnappings. My theory is that race is at the bottom of the Trump phenomenon, too. That at the end of the day race overwhelms everything else: Class, education, income, religion. We’ll talk about that more soon. But in the meantime I’d be interested in your thoughts. "That at the end of the day race overwhelms everything else: Class, education, income, religion." This has and will continue to be true. American white Christian nationalists happily deport fellow christians who are brown because race trumps religion. American white christian nationalists will side with the corrupt oligarchs who run the GOP--even if it fucks up their community with a data center, fucks their budget with tariffs and higher gas prices, and protects pedos on the Epstein List--because it is the political party emphasizes deportations of brown people at home and bombing brown people abroad. They will literally lose their own money, put a data center in their own backyard, and help protect pedos with their vote if it means they get to punish brown people wherever they live. Want a good example? There is a reason Trumpers won't denounce Mehmet/Doctor Oz being in the Trump cabinet as a muslim in control of their medicare--because he's white--while they will scream into every corner of the universe how Michigan will somehow become a state under Sharia Law if Al Saed wins a senate seat there (because he's brown). Proud to have been a donor, but especially proud of this community. The real work is being done on the ground but also from afar by shining a light. We must protect those more vulnerable than us. Always. And we have to call out the blatant racism at every turn, because it is so much of how we got here. I had planned this question for Columbia or Charlotte (coming to both!) but I will ask it here. Who are the first 5 you want to see in our generation’s Nuremberg trials? Emergency Triad: The United States commits imperial suicide. Tim Miller takes on the viral confrontation between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and a protester at a DC wine bar, and makes the case that public officials don’t get to cause mass suffering and still expect polite silence in public. Plus: What a blockade really means, and how Putin’s propagandists are handling Hungary’s election... One part junk science, two parts incompetent government, and with a dash of blasphemy, for seasoning. title: ACC Preview #18 - Duke, Part V: The Offense Should Be A Blast - Duke Basketball Report
content: #1 - UNC || #2 - NC State || #3 - Wake Forest || #4 - Virginia || #5 - #Clemson||#6 - Miami || #7 - Louisville || #8 - Pitt || #9 - Georgia Tech || #10 - Syracuse || #11 - Boston College || #12 - Virginia Tech || #13 - Florida State || #14 - Notre Dame || #15 - SMU || #16 - Cal || #17 - Stanford || #18 - Duke Part I || Duke Part II || Duke Part III || Duke Part IV As we’ve covered previously, Duke has put together a ridiculously deep roster with a lot of experience, size, and immense defensive potential. So what happens with the offense? Add Duke Basketball Report as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. As some have pointed out, there is no Cooper Flagg or Cameron Boozer this year, and while that’s true, it may not matter as much as people think. Like his predecessor, Mike Krzyzewski, Jon Scheyer allows his players a lot of freedom on offense. We really appreciate that. Not to pick on anyone, but when Michigan’s John Beilein took the Cleveland Cavaliers job, we were highly skeptical. He was a superb coach, but he ran pretty rigid plays. Great plays, great results, but that wasn’t to our taste, and we were pretty sure it wouldn’t be popular in the NBA. Players should play without looking over at the bench to see what the coach wants. So what is he working with in this group? Well, a lot. Let’s start with the big guys. Patrick Ngongba II, assuming he stays healthy, is a remarkably skilled big man. He converts about 72% of his shots near the basket and hit 60.6% from the floor last season. He’s quite strong, which is obviously an asset. Duke could also play him in the high post to take advantage of his brilliant passing skills. He gives Duke tremendous flexibility and allows the team to mix things up quickly. Much like Cameron Boozer last year, Cameron Williams will benefit from Ngongba’s presence. He runs really well and will get a lot of lobs from Ngongba and others. He can also step out and score, and as he gets stronger, he’s going to be very difficult to deal with. Like Ngongba, he’s also a good rebounder and should do well on follow-up baskets. He’ll likely be on the court with at least one other big, so Duke will get a lot of flexibility. Drew Scharnowski, the 6-10 transfer from Belmont, is getting over a knee injury but should be ready to go around the beginning of the season. He’s almost certainly the most powerful big on the roster, and while his offense is almost entirely around the basket, he’s an excellent passer. He’ll score, but he’s most likely more of an asset as a rebounder and defender. The big surprise, no pun intended, came when Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje committed on April 30, a month and a day after UConn eliminated Duke from the NCAA Tournament. The basketball cognoscenti was well aware of Boumtje Boumtje, but most fans were not. That changed quickly. When fans saw the videos of his game, it was impressive, and when he had a tremendous showing in the FIBA U17, the assessments shot way up. A lot of analysts slotted him in as the No. 1 pick in the 2028 NBA Draft. It’s a bit early for that, but clearly he’s made an impression. This is interesting too: Duke is listing him at 7-2, which means he’s still growing (he cleared this up on Duke’s Media Day: in shoes, he’s 7-1 1/2). But despite his great height, Boumtje Boumtje isn’t a center. He’s more of a stretch four. The lefty has a sweet stroke, and he’s going to be deadly coming off screens. He’s going to draw a ton of attention when he’s in the game, and that will make life easier for everyone else. He’s probably going to be judged against Cooper Flagg and Cameron Boozer, but that’s not entirely fair, because he’s a very different player than either of them. It won’t surprise us if he emerges as a dominant player relatively quickly. He’s immensely talented and, like Flagg and Boozer, is well ahead of the curve for his age. Duke also has Maxime Meyer, who will probably be further down the rotation as a freshman. He needs to muscle up, but that should happen over the next year. He’s eventually going to be a pain. However, he runs well for a big man and could build a role inside. More than likely, we’ll see a lot more of him as a sophomore when he should pair beautifully with Boumtje Boumtje. We’re not sure what Sebastian Wilkins’ role will be this year, but he can run, he can slash, and he is a solid athlete. He’ll be a useful weapon on the break. Like a lot of Scheyer’s big-man recruits, Wilkins has an instinct to pass, and reportedly his outside shot will be useful too. Given Duke’s size, Wilkins would probably slot in as a wing, which is good, because the Blue Devils don’t have that many, at least not by any traditional definition. However, the wings they do have are dangerous, not least of all Dame Sarr. Sarr emerged as an astonishing defender last season. At 6-8, Scheyer often sicced him on the other team’s ballhandler, and he was the best at that we’ve seen at Duke since Tre Jones. Offense was a different story. Sarr was somewhat spindly last year and had a tough time when he was closely guarded, notably in transition. Well, after this past season, he clearly lived in the weight room, and the Sarr we see now is not the Sarr we saw then. He’s changed his body rather dramatically, and that should lead to much more confidence when he drives. He showed last season that he could shoot the three. Add in enough power to take people to the rack, and his role will change, possibly a lot. The other promising young wing is Bryson Howard. Some people have already pegged him as a lottery pick. Why? Well, he clearly has the talent to play at that level. He is also an outstanding shooter and hit 46.2% of his threes on Nike’s EYBL circuit. He’s got serious range, too. He’s really an efficient scorer, and when he’s in, it’ll make it much tougher for teams to lock down the inside. He’s going to be a huge factor on the break, too. When Sarr gets his mitts on the ball and starts to run, Howard will be a major target. He’s rangy, he’s got a 6-11 wingspan, and he can move. We haven’t seen his vertical posted yet, but his standing reach is probably between 8-7 and 8-9. If his vertical is, say, 30 inches, that gets his hands about a foot above the rim. But what if it’s higher? Say 36 inches? That puts him around the top of the square and about 4 inches short of the top of the backboard. That’s going to make him very difficult to guard. And that brings us to the four-headed backcourt of Caleb Foster, Cayden Boozer, transfer John Blackwell, and Deron Rippey. Foster is arguably the least effective of the four offensively, but that’s not an insult. It’s just that the talent level is extraordinarily high. And keep in mind that, even on a broken foot, he blew the St. John’s game wide open, scoring 11 points when needed, including 7 straight. He’s quite capable. Boozer emerged as a very canny guard late last season, and when Foster went down, he really came through. He looks like he’s really redefined his body, and that will help a lot. We love his game. He should have a great year. Blackwell comes over from Wisconsin, where he had a tremendous career. He averaged 19.1 ppg for the Badgers last year and has a helpful knack of getting to the line. He also has a real clutch instinct, and who can’t use that? He also seems to be showing signs of leadership, which is also great. He’s going to be a huge asset, and his experience will be helpful too. Then there’s Deron Rippey. At 6-3, he may be the best athlete on the team, and with Williams, Boumtje Boumtje, Sarr, and Howard, that’s saying something. During Duke’s Media Day, assistant coach Tyler Thornton said that Rippey’s become something of a sponge and really wants to get better. He has gifts that no one else on this team has, and there will be times this year when he takes people’s breath away. With tremendous quickness, speed, and a 40-inch vertical, Rippey is going to be very difficult to contain. The concern is how quickly he adjusts to the college game. This is a guy who knows he can basically jump over people, but as you move up the ladder, you learn that that’s not enough. He’s going to have to learn how and when to go for the kill, and when to let someone else do it. And with this group, there will always be someone else who can do it, too. There are another two guards on the roster: Jacob Theodosiou and Nick Arnold. Theodosiou emerged as a very solid player at Loyola Maryland. He averaged 13.0 points, 3.8 rebounds, and 2.7 assists per game last year and played in 58 games for Loyola, starting 49. He shoots well and is a smart and disciplined player. A lot of what he does will be behind the scenes, but it’s still important. And he’s also insurance. Hopefully Duke won’t need it, but it’s there if so. Arnold is a preferred walk-on who drew attention for his effort, his hard-nosed approach, and his character. When you put it all together, Duke has a lot of options. Want to go huge? You could put out Ngongba, Williams, Boumtje Boumtje, Sarr, and Foster. Want pressure? Okay. How about Sarr, Howard, Foster, Rippey, Wilkins, and Ngongba? Three-point shooting? No problem: Blackwell, Sarr, Howard, Foster, and Boumtje Boumtje. Want to just run? How about Sarr, Rippey, Howard, Williams, and a big to be named later? This Duke team, to sum it up, is deep, versatile, and gifted. No weaknesses, right? Well, there is at least one to worry about, and it’s important: free-throw shooting. Of the guys who played college ball last year, Blackwell shot 85.9%, Boozer 81.3%, Theodosiou shot a respectable 71.3%, Ngongba 69.4%… and then things go off the rails. Foster shot a surprisingly poor 58.5%, Sarr shot 52%, and Scharnowski just 43.6%. It’s hard to know how the freshmen will do, but certainly Boumtje Boumtje, Williams, and Howard should be competent from the line. There’s no reason why Rippey shouldn’t do well, either. We’ll have to wait on redshirt Wilkins and also Meyer, but freshmen are freshmen, and you just can’t tell ahead of time. Take the most cold-blooded Blue Devil of all time, Christian Laettner: as a freshman, down 77-75 against Arizona with just one second left, Laettner stepped up to the line and missed the front end of a one-and-one. Freshmen—you just never know. Hopefully this won’t be a fatal flaw, but it certainly could be. That aside, this Duke team is going to be fascinating to watch.
